title: AQA GCSE Physics · Atomic Structure and Radiation (part 1)

items.stem: Which of these is closest to the radius of a typical atom?

options.text: About 1 x 10^-10 m, a ten-billionth of a metre
About 1 x 10^-15 m, the size of a nucleus
About 1 x 10^-6 m, a thousandth of a mm
About 1 x 10^-3 m, the width of a pin head

items.why: The specification gives the radius of an atom as about 1 x 10^-10 metres.

items.stem: Which statement describes the basic structure of an atom?

options.text: A positive nucleus of protons and electrons, with neutrons outside
A positive nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons
A negative nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons outside it
A core of neutrons only, with protons and electrons around it

items.why: This is the structure given in the specification: a positively charged nucleus composed of protons and neutrons, surrounded by negatively charged electrons.

items.stem: How does the radius of a nucleus compare with the radius of the atom?

options.text: It is about 1/10 of the atom's radius, as pictured
It is roughly 1/100 of the atom's radius in all atoms
It is less than 1/10 000 of the atom's radius
It is about half of the atom's whole radius

items.why: The specification states that the radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of an atom.

items.stem: Where is nearly all of the mass of an atom found?

options.text: In the electrons, because there are so many of them
Spread out evenly throughout the atom's volume
In the nucleus, which holds the protons only
In the nucleus, in the protons and neutrons

items.why: Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.

items.stem: An electron in an atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation. What happens to that electron?

options.text: It moves closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level
It moves further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level
It escapes the atom, leaving behind a positive ion
It stays where it is but orbits a little quicker

items.why: Absorption of electromagnetic radiation moves an electron further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level.

items.stem: An atom emits electromagnetic radiation. What has one of its electrons done?

options.text: Moved further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level
Left the atom, carrying the energy away with it
Moved closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level
Settled at a new distance of its own choosing

items.why: Emission of electromagnetic radiation accompanies an electron moving closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level.

items.stem: Why does an atom have no overall electrical charge?

options.text: Its neutrons cancel out the charge of the protons
It has just as many electrons as it has neutrons
Its charges are much too small to be noticed
It has equal numbers of protons and electrons

items.why: In an atom the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons, so the charges cancel.

items.stem: What is the atomic number of an element?

options.text: The number of protons in the nucleus
The number of protons and neutrons added
The number of electrons in the outer shell
The number of neutrons in the nucleus

items.why: The number of protons in an atom of an element is called its atomic number.

items.stem: What does the mass number of an atom tell you?

options.text: The number of neutrons in the nucleus of the atom
The number of protons and electrons in the atom
The total number of protons and neutrons in the atom
The mass of a single atom, measured in grams

items.why: The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom is called its mass number.

items.stem: An atom of sodium has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. How many neutrons are in its nucleus?

options.text: 11 neutrons, since 11 is the smaller number
34 neutrons, found from 23 + 11 = 34
23 neutrons, the larger of the numbers
12 neutrons, worked out from 23 - 11 = 12

items.why: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = 23 - 11 = 12.

items.stem: In the conventional representation of an atom, what does the lower number stand for?

options.text: The atomic number, which counts the protons
The mass number, the protons plus the neutrons
The number of neutrons found inside the nucleus
The charge held by the nucleus in coulombs

items.why: The lower number is the atomic number: the number of protons in the atom.

items.stem: What are isotopes of an element?

options.text: Atoms which have different numbers of protons
Atoms with equal protons, unequal neutrons
Atoms of the element that have lost an electron
Atoms of two different elements with the same mass

items.why: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called isotopes of that element.

items.stem: How does an atom turn into a positive ion?

options.text: By gaining one or more electrons from elsewhere
By gaining one extra proton into its nucleus
By losing one neutron from its own nucleus
By losing one or more electrons from its outer shell

items.why: Atoms turn into positive ions if they lose one or more outer electrons.

items.stem: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are isotopes. Which statement about them is correct?

options.text: They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers
They have different atomic numbers and different mass numbers
They have the same mass number but a different charge
They have different numbers of electrons in an atom

items.why: Isotopes of an element share the proton number and therefore the atomic number, but differ in neutrons and so in mass number.

items.stem: A lithium atom with mass number 7 and atomic number 3 loses one electron. What is the resulting ion?

options.text: Charge -1, because one electron has been removed
Charge +1, mass number is still 7, 3 protons
Charge +1, mass number 6, with 3 protons still
Charge +1, mass number 8, a proton joined

items.why: Losing one electron leaves one more proton than electron, so the charge is +1. The nucleus is untouched, so mass number 7 and 3 protons remain.

items.stem: What should happen to an accepted scientific model when new experimental evidence does not fit it?

options.text: The model is kept, since it is proved
The evidence is put down to an error
The model is changed or is replaced
The model is kept and the result ignored

items.why: New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.

items.stem: How were atoms described before the discovery of the electron?

options.text: As tiny spheres that could not be divided at all
As tiny spheres with a nucleus at their centre
As balls of positive charge full of electrons
As clouds of charge with no definite shape

items.why: Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.

items.stem: What did the plum pudding model suggest about the atom?

options.text: The atom has a small positive nucleus with electrons orbiting
The atom is a ball of positive charge with electrons in it
The atom is a ball of negative charge with protons in it
The atom is a solid sphere that cannot be split at all

items.why: The plum pudding model suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

items.stem: In the alpha particle scattering experiment, what happened to most of the alpha particles?

options.text: They bounced straight back from the metal foil
They were deflected by exactly the same angle
They passed straight through the metal foil
They were absorbed and stopped in the foil

items.why: Most alpha particles passed straight through, which showed that the atom is mostly empty space.

items.stem: What is the key difference between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model?

options.text: The nuclear model has the electrons embedded in charge
The plum pudding model has a nucleus at its centre
The plum pudding model gave the atom a net charge
The nuclear model puts the charge at the centre

items.why: In the nuclear model the mass of an atom is concentrated at the centre and that nucleus is charged, rather than the charge being spread through the whole atom.

items.stem: What did Niels Bohr add to the nuclear model of the atom?

options.text: Electrons may orbit the nucleus at any distance
Electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances only
The nucleus lies at the centre and holds the mass
The nucleus contains neutrons as well as protons

items.why: Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances, and his calculations agreed with observations.

items.stem: Later experiments showed that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided. What followed from this?

options.text: The nuclear charge was shown to be a single indivisible lump
The neutron was named, a particle carrying no charge
The proton was named, each carrying equal positive charge
The nucleus itself was shown to be negatively charged

items.why: The charge was found to be a whole number of equal smaller particles, and the name proton was given to these particles.

items.stem: What did the experimental work of James Chadwick provide evidence for?

options.text: The existence of a nucleus in every atom
The existence of protons inside all atomic nuclei
The existence of electron energy levels in atoms
The existence of neutrons within the nucleus

items.why: Chadwick's experimental work provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus.

items.stem: Why did the scattering experiment lead scientists to change the model of the atom?

options.text: A few alpha particles bounced back, which the old model forbade
Scientists preferred the newer picture because it was simpler to draw
Every alpha particle bounced back, showing the atom is solid all through
Nearly all the alpha particles bounced straight back off the foil

items.why: A ball of evenly spread positive charge could not repel a fast alpha particle backwards, so the evidence forced a new model with a tiny, dense, charged nucleus.

items.stem: A rock sample contains unstable nuclei. Which statement best describes radioactive decay?

options.text: An unstable nucleus gives out radiation at random as it changes to become more stable.
Each unstable nucleus gives out its radiation at a time that can be predicted.
A nucleus gives out radiation only after the rock has been heated strongly.
Electrons dropping closer to the nucleus give out the radiation here.

items.why: Matches the specification: unstable nuclei give out radiation as they become more stable, and the process is random.

items.stem: A teacher says that the activity of a source is falling. What does activity mean?

options.text: The number of decays a nearby detector records each second.
The rate at which unstable nuclei in a source decay.
The energy released by each decay in this source.
The time in which a source fully decays away.

items.why: The specification defines activity as the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays.

items.stem: The activity of a source is given as 480 Bq. What does the becquerel measure?

options.text: The energy the radiation from a source gives out each second.
The number of counts a Geiger-Muller tube records each minute.
The number of decays that happen in a source each second.
The time taken for a source to fully decay away.

items.why: One becquerel is one decay each second, so Bq measures activity.

items.stem: A student monitors a source with a Geiger-Muller tube. What is the count-rate?

options.text: The number of nuclei that decay in the whole source each second.
The energy given to the Geiger-Muller tube by radiation each second.
The number of decays the tube records, which is the activity.
The number of decays recorded each second by the detector.

items.why: The specification's definition of count-rate exactly.

items.stem: Which list gives the types of nuclear radiation that an unstable nucleus may emit?

options.text: Alpha particles, beta particles, X-rays and neutrons.
Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and neutrons.
Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and protons.
Alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays only.

items.why: These are the four emissions listed by the specification.

items.stem: What is an alpha particle made of?

options.text: Two protons and two neutrons with two electrons in orbit around them.
A single fast electron that has been thrown out of the nucleus.
Two neutrons and two protons, which is the same as a helium nucleus.
Two protons only, which is why the charge falls by two.

items.why: The specification's own description of an alpha particle.

items.stem: How do the properties of alpha radiation compare with those of beta and gamma?

options.text: It is the most penetrating radiation and travels furthest in air.
It is the least ionising but has the longest range in air.
It ionises strongly and travels several metres through the air.
It ionises most strongly and is stopped by a sheet of paper.

items.why: Alpha has the greatest ionising power, the shortest range in air and the least penetration.

items.stem: What is a beta particle, and where does it come from?

options.text: A high speed electron ejected as a neutron turns into a proton.
A high speed electron knocked out of one of the outer electron shells.
An electron that had already been stored inside the nucleus itself.
A high speed electron released as a proton turns into a neutron.

items.why: The specification's own description of a beta particle.

items.stem: A beta source is placed near a detector and different absorbers are tried. Which description of beta radiation is correct?

options.text: It is less penetrating than alpha because it is a lighter particle.
It ionises more strongly than an alpha particle and is stopped by card.
It is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium and travels about a metre in air.
It passes right through aluminium and is only reduced by thick lead.

items.why: Beta's penetration and range in air, the two properties the specification requires.

items.stem: What is a gamma ray?

options.text: A heavy particle with no charge that is thrown out of the nucleus.
Radiation given out when an electron moves between two shells.
A tiny uncharged particle shot out from inside the nucleus.
Electromagnetic radiation given out from the nucleus of an atom.

items.why: The specification's own description of a gamma ray.

items.stem: Which statement about gamma radiation is correct?

options.text: It is the least ionising radiation and the most penetrating one.
It is the most ionising radiation because it penetrates the furthest.
It is completely absorbed by a thin sheet of lead or thin concrete.
It has the shortest range in air of the three radiations.

items.why: Gamma has the lowest ionising power, the greatest penetration and the longest range in air.

items.stem: Some unstable nuclei emit a neutron. Which statement about this emission is correct?

options.text: A neutron cannot leave a nucleus, so this must really be beta decay.
A neutron (n) is one of the nuclear radiations a nucleus emits.
The neutron carries a negative charge out of the nucleus with it.
Neutron emission is another name for the release of a gamma ray.

items.why: The specification lists a neutron (n) as one of the possible emissions.

items.stem: In a smoke alarm the radiation crosses a small gap in air and is absorbed when smoke enters the gap. Which source is best, and why?

options.text: Gamma, because it is the most penetrating and always reaches the sensor.
Gamma, because the most penetrating source is always the best choice.
Gamma, because alpha is too weak to cross even a small air gap.
Alpha, because it ionises strongly and is absorbed over a short range in air.

items.why: Alpha's strong ionisation and few-centimetre range mean smoke in the gap changes the reading.

items.stem: A paper mill measures the thickness of paper by detecting radiation that passes through it. Which source should be chosen?

options.text: Beta, because the amount getting through changes as the thickness changes.
Alpha, because it ionises most strongly and gives the largest reading of all.
Gamma, because it passes through the paper without being changed.
Alpha, because it is the safest radiation for the workers to be near.

items.why: Paper partly absorbs beta, so the count-rate responds to small changes in thickness.

items.stem: A tracer is injected into a patient and its progress is followed by a detector held outside the body. Which source is most suitable?

options.text: An alpha emitter, because alpha ionises most and is the easiest to detect.
A gamma emitter, because gamma passes out through the body tissue.
An alpha emitter, because paper stops alpha so it is harmless inside.
A beta emitter, because beta is stopped by skin and stays inside.

items.why: Only gamma is penetrating enough to leave the body and reach an external detector.

items.stem: In a nuclear equation, which symbol represents an alpha particle?

options.text: The symbol ²₄He, with the 2 written above the 4.
The symbol ⁰₋₁e, an electron from the nucleus.
The symbol ⁴₂He, which is a helium nucleus.
The symbol ¹₁H, which is a single proton leaving.

items.why: The specification represents an alpha particle by ⁴₂He.

items.stem: Which symbol is used for a beta particle in a nuclear equation?

options.text: ⁰₋₁e, so the mass number is 0 and the charge is −1.
⁰₊₁e, so the mass number is 0 and charge is +1.
¹₋₁e, giving a mass number of 1 and charge −1.
¹₁p, so the mass number is 1 and the charge is +1.

items.why: The specification represents a beta particle by ⁰₋₁e.

items.stem: A nucleus emits an alpha particle. How do its mass number and atomic number change?

options.text: The mass number falls by 2 and so does the atomic number.
The mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2.
The mass number falls by 4 but the atomic number does not.
The mass number falls by 1 and the atomic number by 2.

items.why: Four nucleons leave, two of which are protons, so both mass and charge decrease.

items.stem: A nucleus emits a beta particle. What happens to the mass and the charge of the nucleus?

options.text: The mass falls by 1 and the charge of the nucleus increases by 1.
The mass does not change and the charge of the nucleus falls by 1.
The mass does not change but the charge increases by 1.
Both the mass and the charge of the nucleus fall by 1.

items.why: A neutron becomes a proton, so the nucleon count holds and the charge rises.

items.stem: When a nuclear equation for alpha decay is balanced, which quantities must be equal on both sides?

options.text: The number of protons only, as neutrons carry no charge.
The mass numbers only, as charge leaves with the alpha.
The number of neutrons on each side of the equation.
The total mass number and the total atomic number.

items.why: Balancing is limited to making the mass numbers and the atomic numbers match.

items.stem: Carbon-14 decays by beta emission: ¹⁴₆C → ᴬZ N + ⁰₋₁e. Which values of A and Z balance this equation?

options.text: A = 13 and Z = 7, since a particle has left the nucleus here.
A = 14 and Z = 7, since the charge rises as the mass stays the same.
A = 14 and Z = 5, since a negative particle has been lost.
A = 13 and Z = 5, since both of the numbers must fall.

items.why: Mass numbers 14 = 14 + 0 and atomic numbers 6 = 7 + (−1) both balance.

items.stem: A nucleus emits a gamma ray. What happens to the mass and the charge of the nucleus?

options.text: The mass number falls a little because energy has been carried off.
The charge falls by one but the mass number is the same.
Neither the mass nor the charge of the nucleus is changed at all.
The mass number falls by four and the charge falls by two.

items.why: A gamma ray has no mass number and no charge, so both numbers are unchanged.

items.stem: Which statement shows that radioactive decay is a random process?

options.text: Each nucleus in the sample decays exactly one half-life after the last.
The decay of the sample speeds up as the number of nuclei drops.
Decay can be started or stopped by heating up the sample.
It is impossible to say which nucleus will decay next, or when.

items.why: Unpredictability of the individual event is exactly what randomness means here.

items.stem: The half-life of an isotope is 6 hours. What does this tell you about a sample of it?

options.text: In 6 hours the count rate from the sample halves.
In 6 hours every nucleus in the sample will have decayed.
In 12 hours the sample will contain no unstable nuclei.
Six hours is half the total time the sample takes to decay.

items.why: The specification defines half-life by the count rate or activity falling to half its initial level.

items.stem: If the decay of each nucleus is random, why does a sample have a definite half-life?

options.text: Because each nucleus waits its turn, so the decays are evenly spread out.
Because every nucleus is timed to decay after the same fixed period.
Because a sample holds so many nuclei that their average behaviour is predictable.
Because each half-life removes half, so two half-lives use up the whole sample.

items.why: Large numbers make the statistics reliable even though each single event is unpredictable.

items.stem: The count rate from a source falls from 800 counts per second to 100 counts per second in 24 minutes. What is the half-life?

options.text: 24 minutes: only one halving takes place
12 minutes: half of the total time
6 minutes: 800 falls to 100 in four
8 minutes: three halvings take place

items.why: 800 to 400 to 200 to 100 is three halvings in 24 minutes, so each takes 8 minutes.

items.stem: (HT only) The emission from a source is measured, and measured again after 4 half-lives have passed. What is the net decline, expressed as a ratio?

options.text: 1 : 16, as the emission halves four times over
1 : 4, as there are four half-lives in total here
16 : 1, since the emission is now sixteen times less
1 : 8, from doubling the four half-lives here

items.why: Four halvings divide the emission by 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16, written 1 : 16.

items.stem: A worker finds radioactive dust on their overalls. Which statement describes the situation correctly?

options.text: This is contamination, but it is only a hazard if the dust can be seen.
This is contamination; the hazard is the decay of the dust.
This is irradiation, and the overalls have now become radioactive.
This is contamination, and the dust is a hazard by touch alone.

items.why: Contamination is the unwanted presence of radioactive atoms, and the hazard is their decay.

items.stem: Fruit is exposed to gamma radiation from a source in order to kill bacteria on it. What happens to the fruit?

options.text: The fruit becomes radioactive and must be stored before it is sold.
The fruit becomes contaminated with atoms from the gamma source.
The fruit is irradiated, so no precautions are needed by workers.
The fruit has been irradiated; it does not become radioactive itself.

items.why: Irradiation is exposure to radiation, and the irradiated object does not become radioactive.

items.stem: Why is an alpha emitter more hazardous inside the body than outside it?

options.text: Inside, its strong ionisation is absorbed by cells; outside, skin stops it.
It is never a hazard inside, because a sheet of paper is able to stop alpha.
Gamma is worse inside the body, because it passes through everything.
Alpha is only a hazard if the source is touched with bare hands.

items.why: Contamination puts the alpha source past the skin, where all of its ionising energy is absorbed.

items.stem: A technician uses a gamma source to irradiate surgical equipment. Which precaution is appropriate?

options.text: None is needed, because irradiated objects do not become radioactive.
Handle the source with tongs and store it in a lead-lined box.
Stand behind a thin sheet of lead, which absorbs the gamma completely.
Rinse the equipment afterwards to wash the radioactivity off.

items.why: Distance and shielding protect against the hazard the source used for irradiation presents.

items.stem: Studies of the effects of radiation on humans are published and shared with other scientists. Why does this matter?

options.text: So that members of the public can vote on whether the work is right.
So that the government decides which findings should be believed.
So that other scientists check the findings by peer review.
So that the researchers are paid for all of the work they did.

items.why: The specification requires findings to be shared so they can be checked by peer review.
